validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: Every load-bearing claim in the proposal checked out against the code rather than being taken on trust: the two dropped `date`s in Account.tsx, `occurrence = today ? ... ` at app.ts:570, `skipNextDate` at :466, the four mobile `onSkip` handlers, the two tests that encode the today-semantics this change overturns, the single `unpaidDates` filter, and `getUpcomingDates`'s dead callers. I also verified the machinery the skip half depends on rather than trusting it: `f('json')` and its null handling in convertOutputType, the views.ts field-list spread that makes the schema entry plus the v_schedules override both mandatory, the additive-migration rule that a nullable column on an existing table passes, and that `schedules_next_date` syncs generically with no registration. The one correction I made is the loop placement in setNextDate — the proposal named the `reset` branch, which is not the arithmetic branch; the bare `setNextDate({id})` from advanceSchedulesService:796 shares the path and a loop written only into `reset` would miss it. What holds this below 80: the JSON-column design for skips is a judgment call that nothing in this checkout has validated, since I could not run a single test (no node_modules in this environment), and two things remain genuinely untraced — how packages/crdt merges a lost update to a new column on schedules_next_date across two devices that skip different occurrences offline, and whether any VRT snapshot covers register Upcoming rows. Neither can fail silently in the dangerous direction, but both are real.
validated_work_order.understanding: Two menu actions on an Upcoming preview row name one occurrence and act on another. `onScheduleAction` (Account.tsx:1558-1594) parses every preview id into `{scheduleId, date}` via `parsePreviewId` and then drops `date` on exactly the `post-transaction-today` and `skip` branches — I read the switch and confirmed it. Server-side, `postTransactionForSchedule` (app.ts:570) computes `const occurrence = today ? schedule.next_date : (date ?? schedule.next_date)`, so `today` discharges the schedule's head whatever the caller named, and `skipNextDate` (app.ts:466-467) is `setNextDate({ id, advance: true })`, which advances the head one step past whatever row was clicked. Acting on the 10/17 row therefore discharges 10/03: a posting un-pays an occurrence still owed, and a skip drops money owed. The two branches are one defect in one switch but not the same amount of work. Posting already has a per-occurrence record — the `schedule_occurrence` stamp, which `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` already filters on — so threading `date` is sufficient. Skipping writes no transaction, so nothing anywhere records that 10/17 will not happen: `next_date` is a single anchor and every occurrence before it has already fallen off. Threading the date is necessary but not sufficient for skip; the handler needs somewhere to write the occurrence down.
validated_work_order.root_cause: `onScheduleAction` discards the occurrence it just parsed on the `post-transaction-today` and `skip` branches, and both server handlers predate the occurrence being part of the request: `postTransactionForSchedule` hard-codes `schedule.next_date` as the discharged occurrence whenever `today` is set, and `skipNextDate` has no occurrence parameter at all. The transport already carries it — the `post-transaction` branch and all four mobile `onPost` handlers already send `date`. The handlers do not read it.
validated_work_order.approach:
Take the first shape the issue offers — thread the parsed occurrence date through both handlers — and complete it. The second offered shape (teaching the preview's `status === 'paid'` shift which occurrence was paid) duplicates a concept the preview already models one filter further down and fixes nothing for skip, where no transaction exists to shift for.

Posting: `post-transaction-today` sends `{id, date, today: true}`; `const occurrence = date ?? schedule.next_date` for both paths, with `today` still deciding the transaction's date and no longer the discharged occurrence. Callers that name no occurrence (the Schedules page sends `{id, today: true}` at schedules/index.tsx:56; `advanceSchedulesService` sends `{id}`) resolve `date` to undefined and are byte-for-byte unchanged. The duplicate guard widens to `if (!today || date != null)` so a named occurrence stays an identity.

Skipping: a nullable `skipped_occurrences` JSON column on `schedules_next_date` (additive migration, id sorting after 1790969762045), exposed as `f('json')` on the schedules schema and `_nd.skipped_occurrences` in the `v_schedules` view — the same shape `next_date` already uses, which is why the schema entry alone is not enough and the view override is required. `skipNextDate({id, date})` keeps today's advance when the date is absent or equals `next_date` (this is what keeps IAC-3 true) and otherwise records the occurrence. `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` filters recorded dates out alongside `isScheduleOccurrencePosted`.

The one place I am correcting the proposal: it says to add the skip-stepping loop "in the advance and reset branches alike" of `setNextDate`. `reset` is not an arithmetic branch — it only chooses which columns `db.update` writes. The sole arithmetic switch is `advance ? getNextDateAfter(...) : getNextDate(dateCond, new Date())` at app.ts:239-241, and the bare `setNextDate({ id })` call from the `paid` branch of `advanceSchedulesService` (app.ts:796) takes that same `getNextDate(...)` path as `reset` does. The loop therefore goes around the `newNextDate` computation itself, unconditionally — one place, covering all three callers — bounded by the same `MAX_ADVANCE_ATTEMPTS` constant `getNextDateAfter` already uses (schedules.ts:396), never replacing the `getNextDateAfter` call. Prune consumed entries in the same `db.update`.

files.change: New additive migration, copied from the shape of 1790969762045_add_schedule_occurrence_to_transactions.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION; ALTER TABLE schedules_next_date ADD COLUMN skipped_occurrences TEXT DEFAULT NULL; COMMIT; — a JSON array of YYYY-MM-DD occurrence dates. Id is a fresh timestamp sorting after 1790969762045.
files.why: A skip writes no transaction, so `schedule_occurrence` cannot carry it. `schedules_next_date` already owns the schedule's date state and already syncs (sync/index.ts:777 folds the table into the `schedules` dataset), so a column here rides existing plumbing instead of adding a synced table. Verified against findAdditiveViolations in schema-diff.ts: a new column on an existing table is only a violation when it is NOT NULL without a DEFAULT, so TEXT DEFAULT NULL passes the post-cutoff additive rule.

files.change: Add `skipped_occurrences: string | null` to DbScheduleNextDate (:170) and `skipped_occurrences: string[] | null` to DbViewSchedule (:352).
files.why: The row type is what the raw SELECT in setNextDate reads back; the view type is what the schedules query hands the client. DbViewSchedule types the parsed array, DbScheduleNextDate the raw JSON text, because the raw SQL read has not been through convertOutputType.

files.change: Add `skipped_occurrences: f('json')` to the `schedules` table schema (:115) and `skipped_occurrences: '_nd.skipped_occurrences'` to the v_schedules view's internal fields (:343).

Verified in schema-helpers.ts:58-82 that convertOutputType returns null for a NULL value and JSON.parses otherwise, so every read site uses `?? []`.
The preview filter reads it off the schedule it is handed. Every schedules query in the app is select('*') — app.ts:559, :620, :686 and useSchedules.ts:216 — so no query or hook changes.

files.change: Three edits. (1) postTransactionForSchedule (:545) — `const occurrence = date ?? schedule.next_date` with no today branch; the transaction's own `date` stays `today ? currentDay() : (date ?? schedule.next_date)`; the duplicate guard becomes `if (!today || date != null)`; rewrite the comment at :565-569 and :580-583, which currently assert that today pays next_date whatever date says. (2) skipNextDate ({id, date}) (:466) — no date, or date === next_date, keeps `setNextDate({ id, advance: true })`; otherwise append the date to skipped_occurrences (dedupe, sort ascending, drop entries at or before next_date) without touching either next-date field. (3) setNextDate (:212) — read skipped_occurrences alongside next_date, wrap the `newNextDate` computation at :239-241 in a bounded loop that repeats `getNextDateAfter(dateCond, candidate)` while the candidate is a recorded skip (bounded by MAX_ADVANCE_ATTEMPTS, never replacing the call), and write the pruned surviving skips in the same `db.update` at :253. The loop is unconditional, covering advance, reset, and the bare `setNextDate({ id })` call at :796.
files.why: This is the server half of both branches, and the loop placement is what keeps the rest of the file correct: with next_date never landing on a skipped occurrence, getStatus, getHasTransactionsQuery and advanceSchedulesService cannot read a skipped occurrence as due and auto-post it. The bare call at :796 takes the same `getNextDate(dateCond, new Date())` path reset does, so a loop written only into the `reset` branch would miss it — that is the correction to the proposal.

qa_script: Start the app with no server and create a fresh budget (yarn start).
Add an on-budget account named Checking.
On Schedules set 'Change upcoming length' to 1 month.
Add a schedule named Paycheck: payee Employer, account Checking, amount 100 (Use 'Make positive'), frequency Weeks, with 'Automatically add transaction' ticked.
Open the Checking register. Confirm 10/03 is Due and 10/10, 10/17, 10/24 and 10/31 are Upcoming.
Select the 10/17 Upcoming row and choose 'Skip next scheduled date'. Confirm 10/17 leaves the register and 10/03, 10/10, 10/24 and 10/31 remain (AC-1).
Select the 10/10 Upcoming row and choose 'Post transaction today'. Confirm exactly one transaction dated today appears, 10/10 leaves the register, and 10/03 is still listed as Due (AC-3).
Select the 10/03 Due row and choose 'Post transaction'. Confirm a second transaction dated 10/03 and no double-paid occurrence (AC-5).
Reload the page and confirm both consumed occurrences stay consumed and 10/24/10/31 are still listed — the skip survived a restart, so it is persisted and not just filtered in memory (AC-2).

Open the Schedules page and confirm Paycheck reads Paid with next_date on 10/24, never on the skipped occurrence, and that its own Post transaction today / Skip next scheduled date still act on next_date (AC-5, AC-7).
Restart the schedule (the Schedules page 'Restart' action) and confirm next_date does not land back on a skipped occurrence (AC-9).
At a mobile viewport, open a preview row's menu and repeat the skip on a later row in the on-budget, off-budget and all-accounts filters; confirm the same one-occurrence change each time (AC-8).
risks: setNextDate is the load-bearing next-date arithmetic for the whole schedules service, and the new bounded loop sits on the path skipNextDate, advanceRecurringScheduleFromNextDate, updateSchedule's resetNextDate branch, and the paid branch of advanceSchedulesService all take. Weekend-solve modes make the step non-obvious: keep the loop after the existing computation, bounded by MAX_ADVANCE_ATTEMPTS, never replacing the getNextDateAfter call.

The migration is additive-only as cross-version sync requires, and I verified a nullable TEXT column on an existing table passes findAdditiveViolations. But an older client that writes schedules_next_date without the column will null a recorded skip out — the same exposure schedule_occurrence carries today, and the loss direction is recoverable (skip it again), never a silently lost payment.

Adding a column to a synced table is the change most likely to surprise additive-migrations.test.ts or a sync fixture that snapshots schedules_next_date; run the core workspace tests before proposing the PR.

Two today-semantics tests encode a decision this issue overturns and must be rewritten, not deleted — a reviewer seeing only the diff should be able to see that IAC-2 is why the comment and the tests flipped.
The client skip payload change reaches four mobile files by copy-paste; a missed one leaves mobile skipping the wrong occurrence while the release note claims otherwise.

Each is its own ticket; touching them here would put unreviewed changes into money and date arithmetic.

A way to undo a skip. Nothing in this issue asks for one and it is a real product question (does undo restore next_date, or drop the occurrence from the list?).
The public API (packages/api) — it exposes updateSchedule, not skip-next-date, so it gains no skip-occurrence surface here.

A dedicated synced table for skips — it would need its own primary key, sync registration and query, where a nullable column on the row that already owns the schedule's date state rides existing plumbing.

The `post-transaction` branch destructures `{ scheduleId, date }` and sends both; the `post-transaction-today` branch destructures only `{ scheduleId }` and sends `{ id, today: true }`; the `skip` branch destructures only `{ scheduleId }` and sends `{ id }`. The date is parsed by `parsePreviewId` and discarded on exactly those two branches.

The `date` parameter is accepted and ignored on that path, by design of a decision this issue overturns.

packages/loot-core/src/server/schedules/app.ts:466-467 — `export async function skipNextDate({ id }) { return setNextDate({ id, advance: true }); }`. No occurrence parameter exists, and setNextDate's `advance` branch computes getNextDateAfter(dateCond, nextDate) — one step past the head, whatever row was clicked.

packages/loot-core/src/server/schedules/app.ts:239-241 and :253-266 — `advance ? getNextDateAfter(dateCond, nextDate) : getNextDate(dateCond, new Date())` is the only arithmetic switch; `reset` merely chooses which columns the `db.update` writes (base_next_date vs local_next_date). Callers are :439 (conditions changed), :446 (resetNextDate), :467 (skip), :661 (advanceRecurringScheduleFromNextDate), and :796 (advanceSchedulesService's paid branch, with neither advance nor reset). This is why the skip-stepping loop belongs around the computation, not inside a 'reset branch'.

This is why both the `f('json')` schema entry and the `_nd.skipped_occurrences` view override are required, and why `next_date`'s existing CASE expression is the precedent.

alternatives_considered.approach: Make the preview's `status === 'paid'` shift account for which occurrence was actually paid (the issue's second offered shape).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The shift exists to hide the head occurrence the stamp filter cannot see, because getHasTransactionsQuery only ever asks about next_date. Teaching it about occurrences duplicates a concept the preview already models one filter below it, and it fixes nothing for skip: with no transaction written there is no paid occurrence to shift for, and next_date would still have moved while 10/17 stayed listed.

alternatives_considered.approach: Record the skip as a transaction row carrying the schedule link and an occurrence stamp (zero-amount, hidden row standing in for 'consumed without a payment').
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It fabricates a transaction the user never made and lies to everything downstream: getHasTransactionsQuery would answer 'paid', hasTransactionForSchedule and advanceSchedulesService would treat it as a payment, and it would surface in exports. The tombstoned variant is worse — executors.ts:105 appends tombstone = 0 to every live query, so it would be invisible to the queries that need to read it.

alternatives_considered.approach: Store the skip as an `exdate` exception on the schedule's date condition in the rule ({start, frequency, patterns, exdates}), which every occurrence computation already funnels through recurConfigToRSchedule.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The date condition is also the rule that MATCHES transactions: a Condition('is'|'isapprox','date',value) builds its RSchedule from that value, so excepting a date silently stops an imported or rule-created transaction on that date from being linked to its schedule — a far wider behavioural change than this bug. It also round-trips badly: ScheduleEditModal rebuilds the value as {start, frequency, patterns} from form fields, so every schedule edit would silently drop the skips.

alternatives_considered.approach: Hide 'Skip next scheduled date' on rows that are not next_date, the way #59 hides it on one-off schedules.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It makes the wrong behaviour unreachable instead of correct and fails IAC-1 outright: the criterion requires the 10/17 row to leave the register while 10/03 and 10/10 stay.

alternatives_considered.approach: Advance next_date to the occurrence after the one that was clicked, so the skipped date falls off the end of the window.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: That is the current bug with an extra step: on the 10/17 row it moves next_date from 10/03 to 10/24 and takes 10/03 and 10/10 with it — the money the user is owed, which is the failure this issue is filed about.

alternatives_considered.approach: Put skipped_occurrences on the `schedules` table rather than on schedules_next_date, leaving the next-date row untouched entirely.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: schedules_next_date is the row that already owns the schedule's mutable date state and already syncs; schedules is joined to it only through the v_schedules view. Putting the column on schedules would mean a second write path to a table that is otherwise updated wholesale by insertWithSchema/updateWithSchema, and it would not sit beside the next_date the loop has to consult. Verified: the schedules table has no skipped_occurrences and its writes go through the schema helpers, so this was a real choice rather than a forced one.

alternatives_considered.approach: Split the issue: land the posting half (small, low risk) and file the skip half separately, since it needs a migration.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The issue states both branches are one defect in one switch and both IACs are on the ticket. Shipping only the posting half leaves Skip next scheduled date silently consuming an occurrence the user never named — the higher-severity of the two, since it drops money rather than mis-dating it.

assumptions: The date parsed out of a preview id is always a real occurrence of that schedule's recurrence, since computeSchedulePreviewTransactions generates those ids from occurrences it built. skipNextDate therefore does not validate date against the recurrence; a stale or malformed value records a date nothing matches and is pruned on the next advance.

A skipped occurrence cannot be reached by any other action: posting it is impossible because the row is no longer previewed, and advanceSchedulesService never reaches it because the setNextDate loop steps over it. This invariant is what makes it safe for skip to be additive rather than something posting has to check — and it is load-bearing, which is why AC-9 tests it directly.

schedules_next_date rows sync generically by column and need no registration in a table list or in mappings.ts — grepped, the only reference outside the schedules app and the AQL view is sync/index.ts:777.
f('json') on a nullable TEXT column yields null for existing rows and a parsed array for new ones, so every read site uses `?? []`.

Extending the duplicate-occurrence guard to `today` when a date was named is a deliberate narrowing of an existing decision, justified because the stamp is the identity the preview matches on. The no-date today path stays unguarded so the Schedules page's and advanceSchedulesService's existing behaviour is preserved where it still holds.

f('json') output reaches computeSchedulePreviewTransactions unfiltered: every schedules query in the app is select('*'), and useSchedules' live query re-runs on the schedules dataset while a skip writes schedules_next_date — so the preview refreshes with no manual refetch.

Posting need not clear a recorded skip: the preview cannot offer both a post and a skip for the same occurrence, and if one somehow arrives the stamp wins the exclusion and the occurrence stays hidden either way.
unknowns: How a skip behaves after a full re-sync from a device that never saw it, and how two devices that each skip a different occurrence offline merge. The column is one JSON value on a row that also carries the next date, so I expect last-writer-wins on the array and a possible lost skip; the occurrence then stays previewed, which is the recoverable direction, but I did not trace packages/crdt's merge for this table to confirm.

Whether schedule.edit round-trips anything being changed — it does not touch skipped_occurrences and updateSchedule only calls setNextDate({reset: true}), which the loop covers, but I did not read schedule-edit-utils.ts end to end to confirm no caller reconstructs the schedules_next_date row wholesale.

Whether any visual-regression snapshot covers register Upcoming rows in a state where an occurrence is skipped. The column is invisible to the UI so I expect no snapshot change, but I could not run yarn vrt in this checkout.

Whether packages/api's updateSchedule path (packages/api/methods.ts) can reset a schedule in a way that interacts with the loop; it delegates to the same handler so I expect no difference, but I did not trace it.
validated_work_order.debate_summary:
There was no critique to judge. plan/critique.json is an empty object — the critic wrote nothing — so this council round had a proposal and no objections, which is the one shape of this job where the arbiter's own reading is the entire check. I did not treat the absence of findings as evidence of a good plan; I re-verified the proposal's load-bearing claims against the code myself, and they all held: the two dropped `date`s in Account.tsx's switch, `occurrence = today ? schedule.next_date : ...` at app.ts:570, `skipNextDate` being a bare `setNextDate({id, advance: true})`, all four mobile `onSkip` handlers hand-parsing while their `onPost` siblings already send `date`, the single `unpaidDates` filter, and the two tests at :1387 and :1512 that encode the today-semantics this issue overturns. I also checked the three pre-existing release notes the issue makes a precondition of the decision, and none of them is contradicted: two describe the plain post-transaction branch this extends, and keep-posted-schedules-paid-today is about advanceSchedulesService, which sends no date and keeps its behaviour.

I verified the skip half's machinery rather than trusting it, and that is where I found one real error. The proposal places the skip-stepping loop "in the advance and reset branches alike" of setNextDate. `reset` is not an arithmetic branch — reading app.ts:239-266, `reset` only selects which columns the `db.update` writes (base_next_date versus local_next_date). The only arithmetic switch is `advance ? getNextDateAfter(...) : getNextDate(dateCond, new Date())`, and the bare `setNextDate({ id })` that advanceSchedulesService's paid branch makes at :796 takes that same `getNextDate(...)` path that the proposal calls the reset branch. A loop written where the proposal says would cover reset and advance and silently miss that caller, which is precisely the path that could auto-post a skipped occurrence. I moved the loop to wrap the `newNextDate` computation itself, added AC-9 to test all three call shapes, and added the corresponding test case. That is the only change I made to the substance.

Everything else in the proposal I checked and kept, including the parts I expected to be wrong. `f('json')` and its null handling are real; the additive-migration rule genuinely permits a nullable column on an existing table while it would not permit a new synced table; `schedules_next_date` really does sync generically with no registration; and the schema-entry-plus-view-override pairing is genuinely both-required, which is easy to get half-right because `next_date` is already in the schema and reads as though the schema alone suffices. I rejected nothing on grounds of taste and there is no disagreement between agents to report, because there was only one agent that produced anything. The honest caveat is the shape of the evidence, not its content: this checkout has no node_modules, so not one of these claims was executed and not one of the tests I specified was run. The plan is well-supported by reading and unverified by running, which is the gap a reviewer should probe first, and it is why I set 76 rather than the proposer's 74 — the correction and the extra checks are real, and the unrun tests are equally real in the other direction.
residual_risks: The setNextDate loop is the highest-consequence piece and is covered only by tests I could not execute. If it is written with the wrong bound, or unbounded against a schedule whose every future occurrence is recorded as skipped, it can spin. MAX_ADVANCE_ATTEMPTS is the bound to reuse; a reviewer should read that loop first.

There is no way to un-skip an occurrence. Once recorded it hides that date until next_date has moved past it and the prune drops it, which for a long-running schedule may be months. Deliberate (undo is out of scope) but worth saying in the PR description rather than discovering in QA.

The skip list is pruned only on the next setNextDate write, so a schedule that is skipped repeatedly and never advances keeps growing the array. Bounded by the number of occurrences a user chooses to skip rather than by anything exponential, but nothing enforces a ceiling.

Cross-version sync: an older client writing schedules_next_date can drop a recorded skip, and a newer client will hide that occurrence from a client that never skipped it. Same class of exposure schedule_occurrence already carries, and the failure direction is 'an occurrence shows again', never 'a payment is lost'.

QA step 9 deliberately reloads the page to prove the skip is persisted rather than filtered in memory. If that step is skipped, the change could pass QA while the column write is silently absent — the persisted record is the one part no purely visual check can see.

Because the critic produced nothing, no adversarial reading of this plan exists. The one defect I found (the loop placement) was found by reading call sites, and there may be another that only surfaces when the code runs.
